In the beginning of humanity's history, before time for us even existed, a young deity (for later whom we've had many names) was administered a test in order to judge worthiness for whatever came next. The test would be a practical demonstration of creation. Using its imagination and intelligence, and hopefully goodwill, it must display its ability to create complex, beautiful things. The deity is given a blank slate wherein he must create.

God comes into existence in the nothingness of a void and begins the test. He starts slow, considering the basics of creation. Looking around he sees it is dark so he declares That there should be light, and creates light. He looks on his first creation and believes it is good, but he knows he can do better. He forms the unformed light into the heavens-- stars thrown across the universe-- and sees that it is good but that he can do better. From the fires of his stars he forges into existence heavier elements, in order to create planetary masses: beautiful marbles of swirling gasses, solids, and liquids. He looks at this new creation and believes it is good but that he could do better. So he went across the Universe and began to create, learning how and experimenting with his creativity. Life, he had found out, was a complex and beautiful creation, and after much trial and error around and in the early stages of the universe, God finally settles upon the third planet from the star Sol, a seemingly perfect area for what he wanted to create next.

He formed the broiling, churning mass of Earth into something more orderly. The molten part he placed into the center of the world, so it's liquid movements could create a field of protection around the planet (a trick he had learned earlier on a different world). He caused the solid part of the world to encase the molten part, to protect life from the heat of the core, and in doing so, cooled the planet enough for gasses to condense on earth's surface, creating seas. It was here that he began to create the complexities that we understand as life.

It started humbly, with simple algae. The algae could consume Sol's energy and multiply. Good, God thought, but he could do better. Fishes, that could live in the ocean, would consume algae or other fish and multiply. Birds, that could live outside of it could consume fish, and multiply. Good, thought God, but I can do better.

He formed up from the bottom of the ocean a great mass of land, above the waves, to give his new life a place where it might thrive through further diversity. On this super-continent, later called Pangaea, he allows the algae to migrate and diversify, turning it into plants of many different shapes, sizes and styles, consuming Sol's energy to multiply. He allows the creatures of the air and sea to migrate and take up a part of the land. Some would consume the plants, others would consume lesser creatures, but they would all multiply. Good he thought, his planet now bustling with activity. It was beautiful, watching the conservation of energy play out through the different systems and subsystems of Earth, the complexity and perfection of it all a testament to his great skill and creativity.

And it was good, but God knew he could do better, and now was the moment he would do it. God designs a Man, a free thinking, free feeling, free-willed being amidst the plants and animals and land and sea. Into this final creation, he gave a part of himself, a spirit. This creature would be the single greatest creation of God's test. The great thing about Man was that it could operate its mind in the same way God could. The creature would be intelligent, self aware, creative and beautiful, a divine entity all to his own, in the very image of God itself, but separate.

God, being Man's creator, names him Adam, and commands him to tend to the animals and forests of earth. Adam, new to the universe, knows nothing else, so he carries out the task appointed to him, happily. But God isn't finished. He has bigger plans. He wants to perform a test on his creation to see if he is worthy of whatever comes next. This is the final test of God, and of Man. So God puts Adam to sleep and creates from his template another human, who he names Eve. She is created for a specific reason, and is part of the test. He then restructures Adam to now have genitals that compliment Eve's, and serve the purpose of reproduction, very much like the rest of the animals of earth. (The irony is that if Adam passes the test, then he will never even use them.)

Therein the place that God placed Adam and Eve, he bestows a tree of great knowledge. The fruit, when consumed, would show Adam his aggressive and dominant characteristics, filling him with Wrath, Greed, Lust, Sloth, Pride, Envy and Gluttony. These concepts were unknown to Adam at that time, because nature was his only experience. Nature has no use for these higher emotions. A clock does not envy.

The only rule of the test was do not eat the fruit.

You see, God possessed all of those things (wrath, pride, etc.) and in his effort to create the most perfect and beautiful creation, allowed his pride to get in the way. He wanted to raise the stakes on his creativity, to show that he could not only create sentient beings, but that he could control them as well, even though they had free will. He wanted to show that his creations loved him so much, that they would never disobey him, no matter how tempted they become because of the free will. It would show that God was ready for whatever came next, and God really wanted to pass the test and move on. And God put everything he had into it, dooming himself.

God told Adam not to eat the fruit, and the whole thing was set in motion. I imagine God was confident that his creations would pass no matter what he threw at them, such was his intelligent design. And when at first they did not eat the fruit, God was pleased, but not satisfied. He then tempts Eve to eat of the tree, coming to her as a serpent, knowing that a serpent was too easy for Adam, and he would never fall for it. But to Eve, being of the sweeter and more submissive (easily led) gender, this would be a worthy test indeed. He tells her that eating the fruit makes one like God and it is a good thing to eat it. Being beautifully naive, she does not need much convincing. To his dismay, she takes his bait, and eats of the fruit. She suddenly loses favor with God. And while this first failure on Eve's part is disappointing to God and not what he wanted to happen, he still hopes that Adam can resist.

She experiences an emotion called jealousy, one she's never had before, shown to her by the fruit. Now Adam was God's favorite, because he hadn't yet disobeyed God. God, in his foresight, created Eve for this exact purpose, should she fail her part of the test. She would take the knowledge of the fruit and go to Adam, using her new emotions to tug at his free will, doing what the serpent could not, and tempt him to eat the fruit. She uses her lust to tempt him, her envy to coerce him, her wrath to shame him, and so on and so forth until finally, Adam, having never been tempted like this before, relents and eats the fruit with Eve.

Adam gained the knowledge of God.

His lust for Eve was realized, and they had sex for the first time. Not knowing any better, they both thought it was good. In fact they thought quite a few things. It certainly felt good, the animals did it to reproduce, why wasn't it good? Why would God want to keep this experience from them? When God returned to Adam and Eve, they covered their genitals in embarrassment, because they now knew what the actual purpose of having them was. This was the knowledge of the fruit.

God knew that his human creations with souls would be in a unique situation to experience life, and as long as they didn't know about everything that God knew, they could in theory live as higher intelligence animals (Demigods, perhaps, a perfect union of spirit and nature), if they actually ever reproduced at all. But God wanted to see and show how perfect his creations were, dooming himself. He made it too hard a test, and Adam and Eve failed.

The consequence of failing is that they would know what sex is, the punishment for having sex was giving birth. Creating life, a very God-like trait, and therefor more tempting to have sex. Sex felt good, a carnal desire tempting them to have sex and bear children. The raising and teaching of the child felt good. Taking care of that which you create is a very God-like trait, and it is therefor more tempting to have sex. Every human after Adam and Eve will have the desire to have sex and make babies because everything about it is biologically convincing you to do so.

It was too hard a test, but God made the punishment hard anyway. The punishment is so total that even he cannot change the course we've been set on. We are sentient, God-like creatures, separate and lesser than god, but with all of his faults as well, and our free will and independence from him is what keeps us (Him) from passing our (His) test.

Humans won't stop having sex, which I guess is the only logical way to redeem our forefather's failures: a complete rejection of the fruit's knowledge, a complete submission to God's will for us to be righteous. Total abstinence is the only way to redeem ourselves, even though without reproduction, eventually humans will die off and be no more. But humans will not stop having sex, so how does that same outcome (total annihilation of humanity) come about if we don't just stop reproducing?

We'll end up killing the earth, and ourselves along with it.

an afterthought:

There have been times in the bible where God had tried to correct his mistakes. Take Moses, trying to lead humans back to righteousness through the choice free-will offers. Take Noah, the only man God considered righteous enough to survive the great flood, designed to take us back to righteousness by force. Other prophets and messiahs come and go, all God's attempt to return humanity back to righteousness.

Maybe the end times will be God's final attempt to end his own test.

On Linux mostly zsh, for which I have an extensive config. My shell is already customized enough for me to feel uncomfortable using a default config. I just miss certain things, like vi-mode or Ctrl-Z mapped to fg (see below). But I also have machines that are using default bash (Gentoo) or pdksh (OpenBSD), and they work well enough for occasional usage that I do not bother installing zsh and my config there.

So this is the Ctrl-Z to fg function for zsh that I stole from the grml config:

function zsh-fg() {
 if (( ${#jobstates} )); then
 zle .push-input
 [[ -o hist_ignore_space ]] && BUFFER=' ' || BUFFER=''
 BUFFER="${BUFFER}fg"
 zle .accept-line
 else
 zle -M 'No background jobs. Doing nothing.'
 fi
}
zle -N zsh-fg
bindkey '^z' zsh-fg

alias ffget='wget -4 --user-agent="Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 5.1; rv:2.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/4.0"'

urldecode() {
 if [ -z $@ ]; then
 perl -pe's/%([a-fA-F0-9]{2,2})/chr(hex($1))/seg' < /dev/stdin
 else
 perl -pe's/%([a-fA-F0-9]{2,2})/chr(hex($1))/seg' <<<"$@"
 echo
 fi
}

getfoo() {
 ffget "$1" "$4" -q -O - | \
 grep "$2" | tr -d \' | \
 sed 's/'"$3"'/\2/' | \
 urldecode | ffget -i -
}

mediafire() {
 getfoo "$1" 'kNO =' '\(.*\)kNO\s=\s"\(.*\)"\(.*\)'
}
